title: French, Japanese scientists share Nobel Prize in Chemistry
summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

image.caption: Henri Kagan, left, and Kenso Soai are shown on a screen at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm after being awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday. (Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency/Reuters)

blocks.text: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
Winners share in a prize totalling the equivalent of $1.7 million Cdn
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news statement. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
Kagan, 95, and born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Saclay in Orsay, France, and Soai, born in Japan in 1950, conducts research at the Tokyo University of Science.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm. They will share in a prize totalling 12 million Swedish ‌crowns ($1.7 million Cdn).

blocks.text: The Nobel Prize in Literature will be announced on Thursday and the peace prize on Friday. The economics prize will be announced Oct. 12.

The Nobel prizes are presented to the laureates on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. The Swedish chemist and entrepreneur dictated in his will that the bulk of his estate should be used to fund "prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind."
